doc.title: Ignacio Berroa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 22, 2021 [interview 2 of 2]

title: First night with Dizzy: no English, hand signals and known repertoire
summary: With Jerry Gonzalez translating, Dizzy gives hand signals for swing, 6/8 and solos, and Berroa knows the tunes.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: How was your English at that time?

My English was zero. Actually it’s a funny part of the story, when Mario called me and he gave me the address and the instructions, I asked him, “Well Mario, you’re going to go with me, you’re going to be there, right?” Because I don’t speak English so how am I going to communicate with Dizzy? And Mario, in a very funny way but he was serious, he said to me, “No, it is too cold out there, I’m not going to leave my apartment so you got it. So that’s your problem.” And so my dear friend Jerry Gonzalez showed up with a car, we put the drums in the car, we drove down to the place and Jerry was my translator. So through Jerry Dizzy was, you know, anyone who had the chance to meet Dizzy knows the kind of human being he was. He was the type of person that always showed respect for everybody and made everybody feel comfortable around him. So Dizzy told Jerry, “You can tell Ignacio not to worry because he doesn’t speak English. Chano and I worked for years and Chano never spoke English and I never spoke Spanish, but we both spoke music. So tell Ignacio that we’re going to talk music” and then he gave me the instructions, very simply instructions. He told Jerry, “You tell Ignacio when I go like this [holds up four fingers] that means 4/4 swing, that when I show him six fingers that means Afro-Cuban 6/8, if I make this signal with my hand, if I close my hand I go like this, that means stop. And then when I point my finger at him that means drums solo. Let’s go.” Because by the time I arrived to the club the club was packed. People were sitting waiting for the drummer to show up. So no time to ask me which tune do you know, what do you want to play. I was not the guest artist. I was there to solve a problem. So we went to the stage and it was perfect. Why? Because I was familiar with the repertoire. I was familiar with “Night in Tunisia,” I was familiar with “Salt Peanuts,” I was familiar with “Woody’N You,” I was familiar with “Manteca,” with “Tin Tin Deo.” I knew — I didn’t know the arrangements but I knew the tunes, so that really saved my life that night.
